content:
Jony Ive and Sam Altman have been hinting for some time about launching an AI hardware device, but it increasingly looks premature. The earliest expected official launch would not be until some time next year.

OpenAI has remained extremely vague about the form factor of its first hardware device, but an interview yesterday seemed to suggest it could be something like a HomePad...

Apple's upcoming 'HomePad'

We have long anticipated that Apple would launch a new smart home device combining a smart speaker with a display. Since it sounds like a hybrid of the HomePod and iPad, we have been calling it the HomePad (though some reports suggest it could be branded as HomePod Touch).

The device could offer options for wall mounting or placing on a kitchen counter or desk, and is very likely to be unveiled alongside the new iPhone launching this September.

OpenAI's mysterious hardware device

Ive and Altman spent a year or so hyping up the upcoming OpenAI hardware device in a rather baffling teaser video. They strongly hinted that the product would be a brand new design never seen before, unlike any existing smart device.

However, independent reporting suggests such talk may be exaggerated even by tech industry standards. Recent reports indicate the product may simply be a smart speaker with a built-in camera, capable of features similar to Visual Intelligence or Ray-Ban Meta glasses.

The latest clue

OpenAI continues to stick with its strategy of mystery, but an interview by Joanna Stern with OpenAI president Greg Brockman yesterday provided at least one potential clue.

When asked about the relevant questions, Brockman threw the question to ChatGPT, but neither denied ChatGPT's answer nor the reports about a speaker that Stern mentioned.

ChatGPT: Look at how I put it — something ambient, low-friction, voice-first but not voice-only, and with clear privacy signals. Stern: So what do you make of the reports calling it a speaker? Brockman: Well, I have to say, we are building an entire family of products, right?

When Stern asked whether the device would need a screen, Brockman replied: 'You'll find out then.' Whether that was a relevant hint or just an offhand remark is hard to say. But I find it interesting that he did not deny the idea. One way to think about it: if speculation is that there will be a screen, but you have no plans to provide one, you should come out and clarify to manage expectations.

You can watch the full interview clip below, then share your thoughts in the comments. If you want to jump straight to the device discussion, start at 6:32.
